subject: Numeracy
title: Heavy and light
objectives: Children will say which of two objects feels heavy and which feels light.
Children will predict which is heavy and check by holding.
content: Feeling and comparing the weight of two objects, and saying which is heavy and which is light.
teachingActivities: Let children hold each object before naming it; use strong body language for heavy and gentle for light; ask them to guess, feel and check.
learnerActivities: Hold, carry and compare objects, sort into heavy and light baskets, and make and check guesses.
resources: A heavy basket (filled with large blocks) and a light basket (filled with scarves)
Balloons and stones too large to swallow
assessment: Check whether each child identifies the heavier object when the difference is clear and makes and checks a guess.
expectedOutcomes: Identifies the heavier object when the difference is clear.
Makes a prediction and checks it.

lessons.title: Feel heavy, feel light
lessons.subject: Numeracy
objectives: Children will hold two objects and say which feels heavy and which feels light.
successCriteria: Points to the heavy one on request
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can compare big and small and long and short and use words such as more and same.
resources: A large stone or a bag of sand and a balloon or scarf
Two baskets, one heavy and one light
lessons.starter: Pick up a heavy bag with a big groan and say "Heavy!" Pick up a scarf and float it and say "Light!" Let the children feel both.
teacherActivities: Hold out the two baskets and let each child lift one in each hand.
Say "This one is heavy. This one is light." Use a deep voice for heavy and a high voice for light.
Ask "Which basket is heavy?" and "Which is light?"
Swap the contents of the baskets without telling the children and ask again.
learnerActivities: Children lift both baskets and feel the difference.
Children copy the voices and the words.
Children point to the correct basket.
Children lift and decide which is heavy now.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Hold out the two baskets and let each child lift one in each hand. Children: Children lift both baskets and feel the difference.
Step 2. Teacher: Say "This one is heavy. This one is light." Use a deep voice for heavy and a high voice for light. Children: Children copy the voices and the words.
Step 3. Teacher: Ask "Which basket is heavy?" and "Which is light?" Children: Children point to the correct basket.
Step 4. Teacher: Swap the contents of the baskets without telling the children and ask again. Children: Children lift and decide which is heavy now.

practical.title: Heavy and light baskets
steps: Place a heavy and a light basket on the floor.
Each child lifts both and says which is heavy.
Move the heavy basket with a friend.
practical.safety: Keep heavy items to a safe weight children can lift with both hands; bend the knees to lift; never carry a heavy item alone.

differentiation.support: Use one very heavy and one very light item, and say the word as the child lifts.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to find a third object that is heavier or lighter than both.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

questions.question: Is the scarf heavy or light?

expectedOutcomes: Says heavy or light with support
lessons.conclusion: Lift the heavy basket together and put it down gently. Then float the scarf and say "Heavy, light."
lessons.homeConnection: Let your child lift a full water bottle and an empty one and say which is heavy.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "hold two objects and say which feels heavy and which feels light" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

learnerFacing.songOrRhyme: Heavy, heavy, down we go. Light, light, up we float.

lessons.title: Guess, feel, check
lessons.subject: Numeracy
objectives: Children will guess which of two objects is heavier and check by holding them.
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can compare big and small and long and short and use words such as more and same.
resources: Pairs of objects: block and sponge, shoe and sock, bag of rice and empty bag
lessons.starter: Show a block and a sponge. Say "Which do you think is heavy? Make a guess, then we will feel."
teacherActivities: Say "I think the block is heavy." Lift both and show your surprise or agreement.
Let a child guess and check with another pair, such as a shoe and a sock.
Ask "Were you right?" and accept a nod or "yes".
Place heavy objects in one basket and light in the other.
learnerActivities: Children watch and say whether the guess was right.
Child guesses, lifts both and says which is heavy.
Child nods or says yes or no.
Children sort objects after lifting them.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Say "I think the block is heavy." Lift both and show your surprise or agreement. Children: Children watch and say whether the guess was right.
Step 2. Teacher: Let a child guess and check with another pair, such as a shoe and a sock. Children: Child guesses, lifts both and says which is heavy.
Step 3. Teacher: Ask "Were you right?" and accept a nod or "yes". Children: Child nods or says yes or no.
Step 4. Teacher: Place heavy objects in one basket and light in the other. Children: Children sort objects after lifting them.

practical.title: Guess and check pairs
steps: Give each pair three pairs of objects.
They guess which is heavier, then lift and check.
They sort into heavy and light baskets.
practical.safety: Use only soft or lightweight objects and moderate weights; keep fingers clear when putting objects down.

differentiation.support: Offer two objects with a very big weight difference and hold both for the child.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to explain: "The stone is heavy because it is big."

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

questions.question: Which one do you think is heavy?
questions.expected: Child points to the one they guess.

questions.question: Were you right?
questions.expected: Yes or no, with a nod.

expectedOutcomes: Makes a guess and checks it
Sorts objects as heavy or light
lessons.conclusion: Count how many heavy and light things there are and say the words together.
lessons.homeConnection: Guess which of two shopping items is heavy and lift them to check.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "guess which of two objects is heavier and check by holding them" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Heavy and light carriers
lessons.subject: Numeracy
objectives: Children will carry heavy and light items from one place to another and say which was harder.
successCriteria: Says heavy or light for each one
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can compare big and small and long and short and use words such as more and same.
resources: Two bags, one heavy, one light
lessons.starter: Say "Mama is carrying shopping from the market. She has a heavy bag and a light bag. Who can help her?"
teacherActivities: Show the two bags and ask a child to carry each to the table.
Ask "Which bag was easy to carry? Which was hard?"
Let children work in pairs to carry the heavy bag together.
Put the light bag on a high shelf and the heavy bag on the floor and ask why.
learnerActivities: Child carries the light bag and the heavy bag and says which was heavy.
Child points to the light and heavy bags.
Pairs carry the heavy bag together and say "heavy".
Children say or gesture that the heavy bag is safer low.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show the two bags and ask a child to carry each to the table. Children: Child carries the light bag and the heavy bag and says which was heavy.
Step 2. Teacher: Ask "Which bag was easy to carry? Which was hard?" Children: Child points to the light and heavy bags.
Step 3. Teacher: Let children work in pairs to carry the heavy bag together. Children: Pairs carry the heavy bag together and say "heavy".
Step 4. Teacher: Put the light bag on a high shelf and the heavy bag on the floor and ask why. Children: Children say or gesture that the heavy bag is safer low.

practical.title: Market carry
steps: Mark a short path with cones.
Children carry a light bag then a heavy bag along the path.
practical.safety: Fill the heavy bag only with soft heavy things such as cloth and a little sand in a closed bag; children carry together and bend their knees; no running.

differentiation.support: Carry the heavy bag with an adult.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to guess which of two bags is heavy by looking, then check by lifting.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

expectedOutcomes: Uses the words heavy and light in play
lessons.conclusion: Put both bags down gently and say "Heavy, light, well done."
lessons.homeConnection: Help carry a light and a heavy shopping bag at home with a grown-up.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "carry heavy and light items from one place to another and say which was harder" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Water bucket and sponge
lessons.subject: Numeracy
objectives: Children will notice that a sponge or cloth is light dry and heavy when wet.
successCriteria: Lifts a dry and a wet sponge
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can compare big and small and long and short and use words such as more and same.
lessons.starter: Hold a dry sponge and say "Light!" Squeeze water into a bowl and say "Now it is heavy! Why?"
teacherActivities: Give each child a dry sponge to hold and say "light".
Let each child dip the sponge in the bucket and hold it up.
Squeeze the sponge over the tray and feel it become light again.
Ask "Why was the wet sponge heavy?" Accept answers such as "water".
learnerActivities: Children hold the dry sponge and say "light".
Children hold the wet sponge and say "heavy".
Children squeeze and feel it get lighter.
Children say "water" or gesture.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Give each child a dry sponge to hold and say "light". Children: Children hold the dry sponge and say "light".
Step 2. Teacher: Let each child dip the sponge in the bucket and hold it up. Children: Children hold the wet sponge and say "heavy".
Step 3. Teacher: Squeeze the sponge over the tray and feel it become light again. Children: Children squeeze and feel it get lighter.
Step 4. Teacher: Ask "Why was the wet sponge heavy?" Accept answers such as "water". Children: Children say "water" or gesture.

practical.title: Wet and dry sponge
steps: Give each pair a bucket of shallow water and two sponges.
Hold a dry sponge and a wet sponge.
practical.safety: Use only shallow water, under adult supervision; wipe spills at once; keep towels ready and wash hands after play.

differentiation.support: Use one sponge and ask "light or heavy?" before and after wetting it.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to guess how heavy a sponge will be when it is full of water.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

expectedOutcomes: Notices that water makes a sponge heavy
lessons.conclusion: Dry hands with the towels and say "Heavy water, light sponge."
lessons.homeConnection: At home, lift a dry cloth and a wet cloth and say which is heavy.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "notice that a sponge or cloth is light dry and heavy when wet" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Weight stations
lessons.subject: Numeracy
objectives: Children will show they can compare weights at three stations.
successCriteria: Makes a guess and checks it
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can compare big and small and long and short and use words such as more and same.
lessons.starter: Sing the heavy and light song and show the three stations.
teacherActivities: Rotate groups every four minutes and observe one station closely.
Ask "Which is heavy?" and "Can you guess before you lift?"
Record each child’s level and take photographs.
learnerActivities: Children play at each station.
Child guesses and checks by lifting.
Children tidy at the signal.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Rotate groups every four minutes and observe one station closely. Children: Children play at each station.
Step 2. Teacher: Ask "Which is heavy?" and "Can you guess before you lift?" Children: Child guesses and checks by lifting.
Step 3. Teacher: Record each child’s level and take photographs. Children: Children tidy at the signal.

practical.title: Station circuit
practical.safety: Use soft and light objects only; keep water supervised; wipe spills at once.

differentiation.extension: Ask a confident child to explain why one object is heavy.

assessment.method: Observe and record Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding for: identifies the heavier object; makes a guess and checks it; uses heavy and light.

questions.question: Can you find a light one?

expectedOutcomes: Has an observation record for Week 7
lessons.conclusion: Sing the heavy and light song and tidy up.
lessons.homeConnection: Ask your child to guess which of two things is heavier.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "show they can compare weights at three stations" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
